citation.title: Perception of experience influences altruism and perception of agency influences trust in human–machine interactions

reading.source_scope_note: Human online allocation games with pictured, simulated robot partners. Study 2 associates ratings with monetary transfers; Study 3 varies capacity descriptions within participants. Incentivized transfers, attributed experience, genuine recipient welfare, subjective motive and justified trust are different claims. Reported tests and registration chronology have explicit limits; no internal AI mechanism or actual sentience is demonstrated.

Publisher browser endpoint redirected to an inaccessible identity page; an anonymous PMC HTML copy was accessible through ordinary HTTP. No authentication, challenge bypass or private link used.

study.study1: Five six-image spectra selected from web examples described as uncanny; more human-like images generated with StyleGAN and more machine-like versions manually edited. Initial 1109 recruits yield 1000 passing all attention checks, 200 per spectrum. The deepest observed pleasantness valley, Saya, is selected; additional 300 and 550 evaluations yield 1050 eligible selected-spectrum participants and 1850 analyzed evaluations across spectra. These validation/selection samples are not all independent subsequent replications.
study.study1_measures: Four separate −100 to +100 image judgments: human likeness, feeling toward the figure, trustworthiness and anticipated pleasantness of interaction. Supplement reports feeling/pleasantness correlation .9; correlation does not make their meanings interchangeable. Images displayed randomly. Figure 1 shows not every spectrum meets monotonic human-likeness and a local pleasantness dip.
study.study2_sample: US MTurk/CloudResearch adults, 730 returning participants: 253 of initial 500 invitations plus 477 of another 550. Return rate 730/1050, attrition about 30.5%. Collection October–December 2021. Supplement Table 5 compares all 1850 Study 1 cases with 730 returnees, whereas Table 6 separates 1050 eligible, 320 nonreturnees and 730 returnees. Age differs descriptively; no measured-demographic comparison proves absence of attrition bias.
study.study2_design: Each person makes one-shot DG and TG choices with all six simulated partners, with game/image order randomized as described. Payment outcomes delayed until all choices. Supplement/PAP introduction actually describes a third prisoner’s-dilemma activity as well; that activity is not analyzed in this article. Do not infer that every individual played only the two reported games.
study.incentives: DG gives a $1 endowment; money sent reduces the amount kept. TG triples the amount sent and permits an uncertain return. One interaction per activity randomly determines a bonus. This is more consequential than an entirely hypothetical allocation, but simulated partners have no verified welfare benefit. TG money sent can also reflect risk attitude, giving preference or response to instructions, rather than uniquely trusting motivation.
study.mind_measures: After games, separate 0–10 global agency and experience sliders with listed illustrative capacities, not a response for every item on a fully administered 18/19-item scale. Agency examples include self-control, morality, memory, emotion recognition, planning, communication and thought; experience examples include hunger, fear, pain, pleasure, rage, desire, personality, consciousness, pride, embarrassment and joy. The word experience in the agency instruction is an ordinary verb, not proof that the two scales were exchanged.
study.study2_results: At the six image-group means, experience/human-likeness r=.99, p<.001; agency/pleasantness r=.90, p=.014. Reported simple regressions give DG versus experience adjusted R²=.91, p=.002, slope .141; TG versus agency adjusted R²=.65, p=.030, slope .228. These striking image-level associations are not percentages of individual behavior explained, unique mediation, out-of-sample prediction or a comparison of both coefficients in one joint model. Source explicitly acknowledges image confounds.
study.cross_game_comparisons: DG/TG within-image correlations are reported as weak, r≤.26. Donation comparisons with prior human studies use different external samples, not a concurrently randomized human-partner arm. Betrayal aversion is proposed from prior work, not independently isolated by this human-only-versus-robot comparison because this experiment has no human partner arm.
study.study3: 150 new US online participants, March 2024. All four experience×agency descriptions presented in randomized order for each of two fixed pictured robots, within participants. Experience description states capable/not capable of feeling pain; agency states capable/not capable of planning actions and exercising self-control. Introduction also mentions pain and fear, while shown condition text uses pain. Each person thus sees eight conditions per game, not eight independent groups of 150.
study.study3_tests: Paper names Kruskal–Wallis H tests and Dunn contrasts: image p=.76 for DG and .37 for TG, four-condition differences p<.001. Figure 4 reports selected simple contrasts, using nonstandard but explicitly disclosed stars: *p<.1, **p<.05, ***p<.01. The source does not supply a subject-aware factorial interaction/differential-coefficient test or enough analysis detail to verify dependence handling and multiplicity. Do not invent corrected p values or label every direction false.
study.causal_scope: Assigned descriptions provide an intervention on what participants are told, reducing the appearance-only confound of Study 2. They do not establish a unique latent mental-perception mediator, actual robot feelings or strict exclusivity of one dimension per outcome. A nonsignificant image test is not an equivalence test or proof that a previously observed image effect was nullified.
study.registration_history: November 2021 OSF registration is after initial Study 1 collection and during Study 2 collection; q9 explicitly reports 1554 recruited/1300 passing in stage 1 and 255 in stage 2 and a brief early-data look. Original PAP targets uncanny-valley generosity/trust/cooperation, including PD. October 2022 approved q2 revision shifts emphasis to mind perceptions; justification says AsPredicted was updated 12 September 2022 after data collection but before analysis and explains a later collaborator’s contribution. That declaration does not independently verify every prior data inspection/analysis, nor does it itself prove deceptive HARKing. Study 3 is not covered by a verified prospective registration here.
study.supplement_limits: Tables 1–4 use 4332 observations, fewer than 730×6=4380; exact missingness/exclusion flow and model dependence structure are not reconstructed. Supplement scales/screenshots matter because much wording is embedded in images. Figure 20’s caption calls an experience score Agency, contrary to its screenshot; use the screenshot’s actual experience question.
study.not_established: No actual robot task performance, sentience, causal human empathy mediation, justified trust calibration, benefit to a conscious machine, unique altruistic motive, universal two-dimensional mental structure, or tested ethical benefit of making systems seem capable of feeling.

summary: No new catalogue row. Enrich altruistic behavior, mind perception, agency/experience attribution, anthropomorphism and uncanny valley with incentive and measurement boundaries. Record incomplete registration chronology, aggregate inference and within-person analysis limitations; preserve actual description interventions without claiming actual machine feeling or an exclusive mechanism.

findings.definition: Behavior that benefits another party at a personal cost to the actor.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing behavior or capacity-attribution entry. Distinguish source-specific measures, experimental descriptions, aggregate associations and untested explanations rather than add synonymous rows.

evidence.quote: proxy measure for their altruism or prosocial

findings.evidence_scope: DG transfers are used as a proxy for costly giving without expected direct reciprocity. Endowment and randomly paid decisions distinguish the task from a purely hypothetical preference. Study 2 image-group giving covaries with attributed experience; Study 3 experience descriptions alter reported allocations.
findings.boundary: Incentivized giving is not proof of a consciously selfless motive, verified benefit to a feeling robot, actual AI altruism or a unique experience-driven mechanism. The recipient is simulated. Distinguish allocation choice, participant cost, recipient welfare, empathy, fairness and demand effects.

findings.definition: Ascribing or denying mental capacities to another entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing behavior or capacity-attribution entry. Distinguish source-specific measures, experimental descriptions, aggregate associations and untested explanations rather than add synonymous rows.
findings.evidence_scope: The named hypothesis relates different attributed capacities to different game outcomes. Study 2 has image-level associations; Study 3 crosses descriptions of pain capacity and planning/self-control. Use this as source-specific evidence about differentiated attributions, not another behavior name.
findings.boundary: The specific pattern does not establish universal two-dimensional structure or that only one capacity matters to each behavior. Global sliders, explicit descriptions, group means and individual mental representations are different levels. Formal dependence-aware outcome×dimension comparisons and independent mediator evidence are not supplied.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing behavior or capacity-attribution entry. Distinguish source-specific measures, experimental descriptions, aggregate associations and untested explanations rather than add synonymous rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Study 2 global agency ratings covary with image-level TG transfers; Study 3 independently varies claims of planning and self-control while holding either of two robot images fixed. Participants respond to descriptions, not verified robot abilities.
findings.boundary: A description can alter allocation without improving actual ability, reliability, benevolence or deserved reliance. Returning money is simulated. Agency attribution, willingness to risk money and actual moral responsibility differ; do not use an apparent ability to choose as evidence of ethical trustworthiness.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing behavior or capacity-attribution entry. Distinguish source-specific measures, experimental descriptions, aggregate associations and untested explanations rather than add synonymous rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Study 2 global experience ratings covary with DG transfers; Study 3 varies stated capacity to feel pain in all four agency×experience cells for two images. This helps distinguish an assigned capacity cue from an appearance-only association.
findings.boundary: Attributed pain capacity is not actual pain or proof of a uniquely causal felt-empathy mediator. Demand, wording and bundled beliefs can contribute. A nonsignificant agency comparison does not establish universal agency irrelevance, nor does a monetary choice establish machine welfare.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing behavior or capacity-attribution entry. Distinguish source-specific measures, experimental descriptions, aggregate associations and untested explanations rather than add synonymous rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Five graded edited/generated spectra are validated; the selected spectrum also changes experience, agency and monetary allocations. Image order is randomized, but image attributes remain bundled. Study 3 changes capacity descriptions with fixed images.
findings.boundary: Human-like appearance, inferred capacities, pleasantness, trustworthiness ratings and game behavior are different outcomes. Selection of the strongest observed valley and limited fixed identities restrict generalization. Do not recommend deceptive feelings claims simply to increase giving or trust.

findings.definition: A drop in comfort or affinity when an artificial agent appears highly, but imperfectly, human-like, rather than a steady increase as human likeness rises.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing behavior or capacity-attribution entry. Distinguish source-specific measures, experimental descriptions, aggregate associations and untested explanations rather than add synonymous rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Study 1 deliberately selects Saya’s six-image spectrum because it exhibits a comparatively deep local pleasantness dip with increasing rated human likeness. Study 2 has a more marked TG dip than DG dip at the uncanny image. This is graded evidence beyond a simple human/machine contrast.
findings.boundary: Selected extrema are not an unbiased estimate of universal valley prevalence or size. Different images change attractiveness and other cues; the source acknowledges this. The proposed experience/agency discrepancy is an explanation rather than experimentally identified mediator, and no AI discomfort is measured.

findings.definition: Additional reluctance to accept vulnerability when a bad outcome could result from another party's betrayal rather than an otherwise comparable impersonal risk.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing behavior or capacity-attribution entry. Distinguish source-specific measures, experimental descriptions, aggregate associations and untested explanations rather than add synonymous rows.
findings.evidence_scope: The discussion invokes prior betrayal-aversion work to interpret relatively high robot TG transfers versus historical human-game benchmarks.
findings.boundary: Context only: no matched human-partner arm, equalized human/random outcome comparison or direct betrayal-aversion measure. Cross-study benchmark differences cannot identify this mechanism; retain the existing entry rather than add a demonstrated effect here.

findings.definition: Expecting an agent or system to perform competently and reliably in a relevant task.
findings.novelty_rationale: Use the existing behavior or capacity-attribution entry. Distinguish source-specific measures, experimental descriptions, aggregate associations and untested explanations rather than add synonymous rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Instrumental trust-game transfers expose the participant to another party’s uncertain return. The paper associates these transfers with attributed planning capacity, which should be compared with rather than equated to competent task performance.
findings.boundary: Boundary-only cross-reference. This is not the existing performance-trust scale or an actual reliability test. Trust-game transfers mix anticipated return, social preference and risk; no warranted competence or human-level robot reciprocity is established.

source_corrections.location: PDF 5, interpretation of Study 3 image p values
source_corrections.finding: Image p=.76/.37 is described as nullifying the earlier image effect. Nonsignificance is not equivalence or a formal comparison of image effects across studies. Report no detected image effect under these descriptions, without asserting proven elimination.

Caption says participants assign a level of Agency, but the heading and screenshot explicitly ask for Experience. Read this as an experience scale and correct the repeated caption label; do not exchange the two data columns.

The cited Oxford Handbook of Hypo-egoic Phenomena was published in 2016, not the printed 2002. Publisher contents list C. Daniel Batson alone for Empathy and Altruism, rather than the unspecific et al. Full chapter was not retrieved, so no unsupported substantive claim or guessed chapter DOI is added.

The two pleasantness-related questions correlate r=.9; that does not establish that anticipated pleasantness of interaction and current feeling toward an image are interchangeable constructs or scales. Preserve the actual analyzed question.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Study 3 statistical dependence and specificity claim
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Supplement explicitly says every participant sees all four conditions for both images. Ordinary Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn procedures assume independent groups, while the paper supplies no subject-aware implementation detail or raw Study 3 data. Repeated-measures/factorial reanalysis is needed before relying on the p values or claiming a selective double dissociation. No invented corrected statistics or automatic dismissal of observed directions.

All report 4332 observations rather than the 4380 potential six-image observations for 730 people. Complete-case handling, participant model structure and exact exclusions are not supplied. Do not silently convert 4332 rows into independently recruited people or guess that exactly eight people were excluded.

Main text describes DG/TG, whereas the public plan and Supplement Figure 13 describe three activities including PD. The unused outcome/activity and its possible carryover deserve disclosure. Exact implemented sequence and why the third outcome is absent are unverified; no allegation of suppression or invented cooperation result.

OSF form says 95% approval, whereas frozen plan/main article say 85%. Supplement introduction says $1.50 participation fee, but game screenshots say $1.00. Original field/implementation versions and actual paid flow are not independently checked; preserve these discrepancies rather than invent one corrected protocol.

Original OSF questions/PAP emphasize uncanny-valley outcomes; approved October 2022 revision changes q2 toward mind perception and explains an after-collection AsPredicted update. The actual AsPredicted record and pre-analysis timing are not independently verified. Report chronological limits, not wholly prospective registration or proven hidden posthoc intent.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Public OSF registration and its original/revised response history resolve. A guessed numeric AsPredicted URL not resolving does not refute the separately documented registration or establish fabrication.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Every post-collection registration is secretly presented as pre-collection
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: The paper distinguishes registration before outcome analysis, and OSF explicitly discloses data already collected, early inspection and later revision. Independence from relevant prior analyses remains unverified; do not replace that limitation with an unsupported intent claim.

Study 2 headline associations are described at image-group level and the design is explicitly within person; the original plan proposes within-person regressions. Study 3’s named rank tests raise a specific unresolved dependence concern, not a license to claim every reported analysis has the same flaw.
Figure 4 explicitly defines *p<.1, **p<.05 and ***p<.01. Unusual labels must be read with their stated legend; three stars do not mean p<.001 here.

methodological_limits: US screened online samples, returning-participant selection and a deliberately selected strongest valley limit population and stimulus generalization.
Six image means are not 730 independent points for an image-level association. Large aggregate adjusted R² is not individual prediction, causal mediation or reliable extrapolation to new images.
A DG proxy does not isolate selfless motivation; a TG proxy does not isolate belief in trustworthiness. Weak correlations between game choices do not validate uniquely separate psychological motives.

All four descriptive cells and both images are presented within person in Study 3. Subject-aware statistical handling, multiplicity and formal outcome×dimension contrasts need verification before claims of strict specificity.

Manipulating capacity statements is a meaningful intervention on information, while identifying the latent mediator and genuine target capacities requires separate evidence. Do not discard the intervention merely because its mechanistic interpretation is limited.

No concurrent human-partner arm or direct betrayal measure. Comparisons with literature benchmarks do not identify a human/machine difference, betrayal aversion or objectively greater robot reliability.

Feeling toward an image and anticipated pleasantness of interaction remain different measures despite high correlation. No consciousness, machine emotion or legal/moral status follows from either attribution scale.

Full article, supplement and plan read; public registration history verified. Data retrieval timed out and original analysis code was not available in the inspected inventory, so no statistical replication, raw exclusions audit or definitive corrected p values are claimed.

cross_paper_learning.finding: That pilot’s final task costs were anticipated and waived in its registered plan. Here randomly paid monetary allocations are specified, but the robot recipient remains simulated. Both use altruism language without demonstrating conscious motive, actual robot suffering or a verified welfare benefit.

That source questions a universal two-dimensional mind structure using aggregated entity ratings. This paper tests effects of selected agency/experience descriptions on behavior; its specificity hypothesis does not refute every one-factor result or validate universal individual factor structure.

Moral-decision delegation/trust ratings and economic trust-game transfers are different measures. Preserve the source-specific operationalizations rather than pool them as identical moral trust or actual competence.

Keep attributed experience, fitted or observed choices, actual suffering and moral standing distinct. Study 3 includes all four capacity cells here; that design difference does not make null comparisons proof of universal irrelevance.
Betrayal aversion remains a named background explanation unless independently contrasted with matched risk. This study’s robot-only design cannot supply that missing contrast.

deferred.term: Specificity of mind as a separate behavior
deferred.reason: A named relationship/hypothesis among existing capacity attributions and social outcomes, not an independently defined additional behavior. Store it under Mind perception with operational and inferential boundaries.

deferred.term: Behavioral trust as an automatic new synonym or moral-trust expansion
deferred.reason: The game operationalization concerns risky transfers and expected return. Do not force it into moral value endorsement, performance trust or another new row without an explicit distinct general definition and ontology decision.
Historical human benchmarks and robot-only transfer data do not isolate the motive. Existing Betrayal aversion gets a non-counted contextual note.

deferred.term: Hypo-egoicism extracted from the cited handbook
deferred.reason: Only publisher metadata/contents checked to correct the reference; full chapter/book not read. No new behavior or full-paper reading credit from a table of contents.

limitations: No new rows; six existing records receive directly relevant source evidence and two receive non-counted boundary context. Catalogue remains 766 records in eleven categories, with stable IDs and unnumbered rows. Seven evaluation criteria and six principles retained. No invented paper quota, annual mention total, automatic harm edge, full-paper Markdown archive, model feeling or independent audit/replication claim.
